PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 92 — Lesson 116: Headache, Migraine & Secondary Headache Red Flags

FNP-level goal: Recognize a primary headache pattern only after actively considering dangerous secondary causes, use targeted rather than reflexive imaging, and build an individualized acute and preventive migraine plan that avoids medication-overuse harm.

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish the usual clinical patterns of migraine, tension-type headache, cluster headache, and medication-overuse headache.
  • Use onset, age, neurologic findings, systemic context, pregnancy status, eye symptoms, trauma, and change in pattern to identify secondary-headache red flags.
  • Recognize thunderclap headache, possible stroke, meningitis, acute angle-closure glaucoma, giant cell arteritis, and pregnancy/postpartum headache as time-sensitive conditions.
  • Apply imaging stewardship: uncomplicated stable primary headache does not automatically require imaging, while red flags change the diagnostic pathway.
  • Create a patient-centered migraine plan that addresses acute treatment, prevention, triggers, disability, contraindications, rescue limits, follow-up, and referral.

Part 1 — Headache Is a Symptom, Not a Diagnosis

The FNP should begin with two questions: Is this a new or changed headache? Could it be secondary to another disease? Most outpatient headaches are primary headache disorders, but the consequences of missing a vascular, infectious, inflammatory, ocular, intracranial-pressure, toxic, or pregnancy-related cause can be severe.

A high-quality history includes first versus recurrent headache, exact onset and time to peak intensity, location, quality, duration, frequency, disability, associated nausea, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, aura, autonomic features, fever, neck symptoms, visual symptoms, positional or exertional relationship, sleep interruption, trauma, medications and substances, pregnancy/postpartum status, cancer, immunocompromise, vascular risk, and family history. Ask what the patient means by worst headache; a severe familiar migraine is different from a sudden maximum-intensity new pain.

Part 2 — Migraine: Diagnose the Pattern, Then Measure Disability

Migraine commonly causes episodic moderate-to-severe headache with activity sensitivity and features such as nausea, photophobia, phonophobia, or sensory symptoms. Pain can be unilateral or bilateral and may be throbbing, but rigid stereotype matching is less useful than recognizing a recurrent, coherent syndrome with normal neurologic examination between attacks and no red flags.

Ask how many headache days occur each month, how many are migraine days, how often acute medication is used, what the patient cannot do during an attack, and how quickly treatment is taken. A calendar or diary can reveal menstrual association, sleep disruption, missed meals, caffeine pattern, stress, neck pain, medication overuse, and treatment response. The goal is not to blame the patient for triggers; it is to identify modifiable patterns and choose realistic prevention.

Part 3 — Other Primary Headache Patterns

Tension-type headache is often bilateral, pressing or tightening, mild-to-moderate, and not strongly worsened by routine activity, although individual presentations vary. Cluster headache is less common but important: severe unilateral orbital or temporal pain occurs in stereotyped attacks with autonomic findings such as tearing, nasal symptoms, eyelid change, or agitation. New unilateral autonomic headache still requires thoughtful assessment because secondary disorders can mimic it.

Do not label every occipital, neck-associated, or sinus-area headache as tension or sinus disease. Migraine often includes neck pain and facial pressure. A diagnosis should explain the whole syndrome and remain open to revision when the pattern changes.

Part 4 — Medication-Overuse Headache

Frequent use of acute headache medication can perpetuate headache frequency and reduce response to therapy. Review all over-the-counter and prescribed products, including combination analgesics, caffeine-containing products, migraine-specific rescue medication, opioids, and medications obtained outside the medical record. A patient may not recognize a daily tablet as a headache treatment if it is called a sleep, sinus, or pain medicine.

Management is not simply telling the patient to stop everything. Explain the cycle, establish safe limits and a bridge or preventive strategy when indicated, address the underlying migraine disorder, and provide follow-up. Withdrawal and discontinuation plans must account for the specific medication, comorbidities, pregnancy possibility, dependence risk, and access to support.

Part 5 — Secondary-Headache Red Flags

Red flags are features that raise concern for intracranial or systemic pathology. Important examples include sudden onset reaching maximal intensity quickly; new focal neurologic deficit, altered mental status, seizure, or syncope; fever or meningismus; papilledema or features of raised intracranial pressure; new headache after age 50; cancer or immunocompromise; pregnancy or postpartum onset; recent trauma; anticoagulation or bleeding risk; exertional or Valsalva-triggered onset; positional change; and progressive worsening or a major change from the patient’s usual pattern.

No mnemonic replaces clinical judgment. A patient with a familiar migraine may still develop stroke, infection, hemorrhage, glaucoma, or another emergency. Conversely, the presence of nausea or light sensitivity does not prove migraine because several dangerous disorders can produce them.

Part 6 — Thunderclap Headache: Treat Time as Data

A thunderclap headache reaches maximal intensity abruptly, often within a minute. It requires emergency evaluation for subarachnoid hemorrhage and other vascular or secondary causes. Record the exact onset time, triggering activity, neurologic symptoms, neck pain, exertion, pregnancy/postpartum context, and medications. Do not send the patient to drive themselves to outpatient imaging or wait for the next available clinic scan when emergency evaluation is indicated.

Sudden severe headache accompanied by weakness, facial asymmetry, speech difficulty, confusion, loss of balance, or acute visual symptoms also triggers stroke pathways. Symptoms that resolve can still represent transient ischemia and require urgent assessment.

Part 7 — The Older Adult With New Headache

New headache after age 50 is a red flag because secondary causes become more likely. Ask specifically about scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, constitutional symptoms, shoulder or hip girdle stiffness, visual symptoms, and temporal-artery tenderness when giant cell arteritis (GCA) is possible. Vision loss from GCA can be irreversible; suspected disease needs urgent evaluation and treatment coordination rather than a routine referral.

Also consider malignancy, medication effects, hypertension-related context without assuming blood pressure is always the cause, sleep apnea, cervical disease, glaucoma, and intracranial processes. The assessment should be broad but prioritized by urgency.

Part 8 — Pregnancy and Postpartum Headache

New, severe, or changing headache in pregnancy or the postpartum period deserves a lower threshold for urgent evaluation. Preeclampsia/eclampsia, cerebral venous thrombosis, hemorrhage, reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome, pituitary disorders, and other conditions can present with headache. Blood pressure, neurologic symptoms, visual symptoms, edema, right-upper-quadrant or epigastric symptoms, and timing relative to delivery matter.

Do not assume a patient has migraine merely because they have a migraine history. Reproductive safety also changes medication selection for both acute and preventive care, requiring current prescribing guidance and shared decision-making.

Part 9 — Imaging Stewardship

Neuroimaging is not routinely required for a stable headache that fits an uncomplicated primary migraine pattern and has no red flags or abnormal neurologic findings. Imaging is not reassurance medicine; it is a diagnostic test that should answer a clinical question. In contrast, red flags, neurologic deficit, new concerning pattern, trauma, cancer or immunocompromise, pregnancy/postpartum context, and suspected vascular or intracranial-pressure disorder often warrant urgent imaging or emergency evaluation according to local pathways.

Choose the care setting before choosing the test. A patient with suspected stroke, hemorrhage, meningitis, acute glaucoma, or thunderclap headache needs emergency-capable evaluation. An outpatient MRI order is not a substitute for emergency triage.

Part 10 — Building a Migraine Plan

A comprehensive plan has four parts. First, confirm the diagnosis and exclude red flags. Second, select acute therapy based on attack severity, nausea, onset, cardiovascular and other contraindications, pregnancy status, previous response, and medication-overuse risk. Third, consider preventive therapy when headache burden, disability, acute-treatment failure, contraindications, or acute-medication frequency make prevention appropriate. Fourth, establish behavioral foundations: regular sleep, hydration, meals, physical activity as tolerated, stress support, and a diary without turning normal life into a list of forbidden triggers.

Set outcome goals such as fewer disabling days, faster return to function, less rescue-medication use, and fewer urgent visits. Review safety, interactions, adverse effects, and a clear plan for when to seek urgent care. Neurology referral is appropriate for diagnostic uncertainty, refractory or complex migraine, chronic migraine, unusual aura, difficult medication selection, or suspected secondary cause after initial assessment.

Part 11 — FNP Case: The Familiar Migraine

A 27-year-old has recurrent headaches with nausea, photophobia, and predictable disability, normal neurologic examinations between episodes, and no change in pattern. The FNP measures monthly headache and acute-medication days, reviews pregnancy plans and contraindications, creates an acute strategy and preventive discussion if burden warrants it, and schedules follow-up. Routine imaging is not automatically required simply because the headaches are severe.

Part 12 — FNP Case: The Headache That Is Not Migraine

A 58-year-old with no migraine history develops a new temporal headache with jaw pain when chewing and brief visual dimming. Even if the pain is not dramatic, the age, new pattern, jaw symptoms, and visual complaint raise concern for GCA. The correct action is urgent evaluation and treatment coordination to protect vision, not a trial of a routine migraine medication and delayed follow-up.

Part 13 — FNP Case: The Daily Rescue Cycle

A patient with migraine now takes several different pain products most days and reports headache on nearly every day. The FNP identifies possible medication overuse, reviews all agents rather than adding another rescue prescription, explains the cycle, establishes a safe individualized reduction and prevention plan, and arranges close follow-up. More analgesic is not always more control.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Characterize: onset, time to peak, pattern change, disability, associated symptoms, and medications.
  2. Screen red flags: thunderclap, neurologic deficit, fever/meningismus, eye danger, age over 50 with new headache, cancer/immunocompromise, trauma, pregnancy/postpartum, progressive or positional pattern.
  3. Choose setting: emergency-capable care for time-sensitive threats; outpatient workup only when stable and appropriate.
  4. Use imaging with purpose: do not image uncomplicated stable migraine reflexively; do not use outpatient imaging to delay emergency care.
  5. Manage migraine longitudinally: acute plan, prevention when indicated, medication-overuse review, behavioral support, and referral when complexity exceeds primary-care management.

Take-Home Summary

Headache care is a triage problem before it is a medication problem. A stable recurrent migraine pattern can be managed thoughtfully without routine imaging, but a thunderclap headache, focal neurologic symptoms, painful red eye with vision change, systemic illness, new older-adult headache, or pregnancy/postpartum change may represent a secondary emergency. The FNP protects patients through a structured history, focused examination, purposeful imaging, safe migraine planning, and explicit return precautions.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace individualized diagnosis, local emergency pathways, current prescribing information, pregnancy-specific guidance, neurology or ophthalmology consultation, or emergency evaluation when red flags are present.
